text_original: Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer finds the E350's 255-hp 2.0-liter mild-hybrid powertrain silky and adequately powerful for the car's purpose. Reviewer states the optional adaptive air suspension soaks up potholes and expansion joints without losing body control. Reviewer finds the brakes touchy, sometimes causing a sudden lurch that surprised passengers. Reviewer praises the optional Superscreen's graphics, processing speed and animations; the passenger screen streams video and goes private while driving. Reviewer praises the cabin's gloss-black, frosted-aluminum and dark-wood trim and the rich optional leather. Reviewer suspects the screen-heavy cockpit, aimed at younger buyers, may not appeal to traditional Mercedes buyers. Reviewer warns that options and packages add up quickly; the loaded test car reached $82,000 against a $63,450 base price. Original excerpt(s), from tool summaries: «a mite touchy»

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer states the narrow rear window limits the view behind and the tall dashboard hurts forward visibility. Reviewer states the low roofline and raised rear cushions put rear passengers' heads against the headliner and make getting in and out awkward. Reviewer finds the 12.8-inch portrait touchscreen tricky to navigate at a glance; it takes many exposures to learn. Reviewer states the digital gauge cluster sits so high that he had to raise the steering wheel and drive with his arms up. Reviewer states the driver-monitoring camera repeatedly asked him to raise the steering wheel, and raising the seat was not possible because of limited headroom under the panoramic roof. Reviewer praises the ride for soaking up bumps. Reviewer finds the cabin very quiet, with little tire, motor or wind noise. Reviewer praises the agility from rear-wheel steering of up to 10 degrees, although steering feel is numb. Reviewer criticizes a dead, uncommunicative brake pedal; with strong regen the pedal moves on its own when lifting off the accelerator. Reviewer criticizes the tall, cliff-like dashboard, especially with the optional Hyperscreen. Original excerpt(s), from tool summaries: «a gunslit of an opening» «massively disconcerting»

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer praises the new 12.3-in touchscreen, moved 4.3 in closer to the driver, which replaces the old non-touch display that was hard to use while driving. Reviewer likes that Apple CarPlay can use the full 12.3-in screen. Reviewer praises the comfort and refinement of the ES 350 V6 on the standard suspension. Reviewer welcomes Lexus Safety System+ 2.5 making blind-spot monitoring and rear cross-traffic alert standard, plus intersection turning assist. Reviewer notes the V6 ES 350 starts at the same price as the four-cylinder ES 250 ($41,875 incl. destination). Reviewer states the backup and 360-degree camera images are distorted and less clear than they should be. Reviewer states lane centering holds its position inconsistently, tending to drift to the right. Reviewer finds the F Sport package rides harsher even with adjustable shocks, and its handling gains are not worth the cost. Reviewer argues the front-drive-only ES 350 V6 needs all-wheel drive, which is offered only on the ES 250.

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Cars.com editors list Super Cruise hands-free driver assistance as a strength of the 2025 CT5. Cars.com editors list the roomy cabin as a strength. Cars.com editors list the ride quality as a strength. Cars.com editors list the new 2025 tech features, including the 33-in display, as a strength. Cars.com editors praise the ferocious acceleration of the CT5-V Blackwing. Cars.com editors find acceleration only so-so with the base turbo four-cylinder. Cars.com editors list the cozy trunk as a weakness. Cars.com editors find back-seat headroom tight for tall adults. Cars.com editors find the interior materials not as upscale as many rivals'.

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer finds the Long Range's acceleration smooth and quite strong. Reviewer states the overhauled suspension gives ride and handling that rival a German sports sedan. Reviewer notes a quieter cabin thanks to added sound deadening and acoustic glass. Reviewer praises the Supercharger experience; Tesla claims up to 185 miles added in about 15 minutes. Reviewer reports the touch-sensitive turn-signal pad sometimes did not work and was easy to press by mistake. Reviewer warns the touchscreen gear selector could be a deal breaker for some buyers; redundant headliner shift buttons act as a backup. Reviewer prefers physical controls to the mostly digital ones and finds the UI restrictive. Reviewer notes meaningful materials upgrades, such as textured cloth replacing the wood veneer. Reviewer states the car feels like good value for the money.

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer finds the dual-motor A6 (456 hp, 0-60 mph in 4.3 s) properly quick, though the S6 does not feel much stronger. Reviewer praises the well-balanced ride on the available adaptive air suspension, comparing it to flying rather than driving. Reviewer finds the car nearly as good in corners as the gas S6. Reviewer finds the steering light and obviously digital, and says the car is not meant to excite. Reviewer praises the strong, impressive braking. Reviewer likes the four regen levels set with steering-wheel paddles, ranging from near one-pedal driving to almost no regen. Reviewer calls the MMI one of the nicer and easier systems to operate: clear, intuitive and responsive. Reviewer notes the only physical controls are a volume knob, a start button and a short rocker shifter, which makes the cabin feel clinical. Reviewer notes the usual luxury materials, such as leather, with microsuede accents in the S6. Reviewer criticizes lofty pricing and too little difference between the A6 and the S6, which costs about $10,800 more than the dual-motor A6.

Collector paraphrase (not verbatim source text): Reviewer (Prestige with Sport Plus) finds the standard 362-hp V6 powerful and Audi's 4.5 s 0-60 mph claim believable. Reviewer finds the seven-speed dual-clutch transmission shifts smoothly. Reviewer finds the car not particularly thrilling or fun to drive, with a bit less emotional warmth than before. Reviewer praises the ride quality and finds the adaptive air suspension rides better than the Sport Plus setup. Reviewer finds the Sport Plus package adds only moderate agility over the standard A6, with cornering ability well beyond what typical buyers need. Reviewer calls the MMI interface one of the best in the industry, with an extensive screen setup. Reviewer dislikes the heavy use of gloss-black surfaces; the page's cons list says the interior feels cheap in places. Reviewer calls the roughly $6,000 rise in base price over the previous model steep, though standard equipment has increased.
